Respiratory diseases: physical examination

17 diseases and their stages: for each, the inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation findings are shown on an anatomical map, with sounds. Sounds are played from a real patient recording where one exists, and from the teaching model otherwise.

Compiled by: Asadbek Axmatkulov · Tashkent State Medical University, Faculty of General Medicine No. 2, 3rd year · Department of Propaedeutics of Internal Diseases No. 2 · 2026

Sound sources
RECORDING

Recordings of real patients: the open SPRSound database (Shanghai Children's Medical Center, CC BY 4.0). Each recording is labeled by specialists according to sound type. Vesicular breathing, whistling (sibilant) and rumbling (sonorous) dry rales, fine and coarse moist rales, stridor.

MODEL

Sounds for which no open recording was found are synthesized in the browser from acoustic parameters: 8 percussion notes, bronchial, mixed, amphoric, harsh and saccadic breathing, crepitation, pleural friction rub.

Listen with earphones or good speakers: the recordings are the sound of a stethoscope, that is, rich in low frequencies.

Examination sequence

Comparative percussion and auscultation: left and right symmetric points in turn.

Where the lobes are heardFrom the front: the right upper and middle lobes (below the 4th rib), the left upper lobe. From the side: all three lobes. From the back: above Th III the upper lobes, below it the lower lobes. That is why lower lobe pneumonia is found mainly from the back and the side.

02 · Examination technique

Palpation, percussion, auscultation

Each method answers one question: is the tissue dense, airy or fluid-filled, and how does it conduct sound. The result is always compared with the symmetric point.

Palpation

Four steps

  1. Painful points: both palms on symmetric areas; ribs, intercostal spaces, muscles, spinous processes. A rib fracture — crepitus; neuralgia — 3 painful points.
  2. Resistance: compression in the anteroposterior (sternum and interscapular area) and lateral directions. Increased in emphysema and exudative pleurisy.
  3. Excursion: palms on the lower lateral areas, thumbs beside the spine; on deep inspiration the fingers should move apart equally.
  4. Vocal fremitus: palms parallel to the ribs, the patient says “thirty-three” or “ninety-nine” in a low voice; the hands are then swapped. Increased — consolidation, cavity; decreased — fluid, air, emphysema; absent — obstructive atelectasis.
Percussion

Finger on finger

  1. The middle phalanx of the left 3rd finger (pleximeter) is pressed firmly to the skin, the other fingers are lifted.
  2. With the right 3rd finger, tap twice, short and perpendicular, using only wrist movement.
  3. Comparative: moderate force; supraclavicular → clavicles → 1st–2nd spaces → axilla 4th–5th → suprascapular → interscapular (pleximeter vertical) → infrascapular 7th–9th.
  4. Topographic: quiet force; from clear sound toward dull; the border is marked at the edge of the pleximeter on the clear-sound side. Apices, Kronig's isthmus, lower borders along 7 lines, mobility (6–8 cm on the midaxillary line).

Percussion detects foci at a depth of 5–7 cm and larger than 2–3 cm, and pleural fluid over 300–500 mL.

Auscultation

With the stethoscope diaphragm

  1. A quiet, warm room; the patient sitting or standing, undressed to the waist. The diaphragm is pressed firmly to the skin, not over clothing.
  2. Deeper, even breathing through the mouth; 1–2 full cycles at each point.
  3. The sequence is the same as in comparative percussion, left and right in turn.
  4. Main breath sound → duration of expiration → adventitious sounds (type, phase, location).
  5. Differentiate: asking the patient to cough, pressing the stethoscope, “false breathing” with the mouth and nose closed.
  6. Bronchophony: whispered “one-two-three”; increased — consolidation and cavity; decreased — fluid, air, atelectasis.

RecordingsZhang Q. et al. SPRSound: Open-Source SJTU Paediatric Respiratory Sound Database. IEEE Trans Biomed Circuits Syst. 2022;16(5):867–881. License: CC BY 4.0. Segments of 5–11 seconds were cut from the recordings, filtered at 80–1600 Hz and loudness-normalized; 3 stethoscope clicks were removed from the vesicular breathing recording; “diminished vesicular breathing” was derived from that recording with −10 dB and a 350 Hz low-pass filter. Because the recordings come from children, the breathing is faster.
ModelsPercussion notes, bronchial, mixed, amphoric, harsh and saccadic breathing, crepitation and pleural friction rub were synthesized from frequency, duration and position in the breath phase, because no openly licensed real recording was found. Compare them in clinical practice and with the recordings in the following libraries: Easy Auscultation, Thinklabs, R.A.L.E.

The text, structure, anatomical maps and interactive parts of this independent work were prepared with the help of the artificial intelligence Claude (Anthropic), based on the textbooks and sources listed. The compiler selected the material, defined the structure and checked it. Before applying the clinical data in practice, it is recommended to compare them with the main textbooks and current clinical protocols.
